findings.title: Turn 1 and the first MOVE pay a one-off lambda and string-concatenation bootstrap under the 50 ms limit
findings.evidence:
Cause. When the queen touches a site on turn 0 (touchedSite=2 or 16 in all 4 inputs I dumped), MainBot.play takes the touched branch (Player.java:1190-1200) and returns BUILD without running any lambda. So the first execution of a lambda happens on turn 1: the IntPredicate at Player.java:1210-1211, via LambdaMetafactory, InnerClassLambdaMetafactory and ASM class spinning. The first loading of Player$Physics (MainBot.nearest -> distSq, line 1164) and of Player$Const (train loop, line 1226) also falls on turn 1.

Class-load log (-Xlog:class+load, seed 500, seat 0, JDK 17.0.12): LambdaMetafactory, IntPredicate, InnerClassLambdaMetafactory, Player$MainBot$$Lambda$1, Player$Physics and Player$Const all load inside the 11.9 ms turn-1 window. Player$MainBot$$Lambda$2 loads at turn 23 (2.4 ms). The first MOVE adds a new string-concatenation recipe ("MOVE " + x + " " + y, line 56) and usually also the threat lambda (line 1203). With -Xint the turn-1 cost is similar (7-10.5 ms), so it comes from interpreted bootstrap work, not from the JIT.

Measurements, 150 games at default flags vs v01 and boss, both seats, AuditRun driver:
- Turn 1: p50 8.19 ms, p90 12.60 ms, max 23.95 ms; above 5 ms in 128 of 150 games.
- First MOVE turn: p50 8.16 ms, max 18.62 ms (109 games).
- Minimal Java bot, interleaved: turn 1 p50 0.34 ms, max 2.52 ms.
- Same pattern on the JBR 25 runtime with --release 21 classes (turn 1 max 17.84 ms).

Under the heavier load of procCheck run 1 the bot itself printed 'SLOW turn 1 45ms', and maxLater vs boss was 47.3 ms.

In 2019, CG staff said the serial GC was in use (t/79118 #13); HotSpot picks that collector when it sees fewer than 2 CPUs. If bots still run on one CPU, the C1 compiles this bootstrap triggers compete with the main thread, and the stall can be longer on CG than here. No timeout was traced to this stall in the 290 instrumented games.

findings.title: procCheck timing is sensitive to CPU load and can accept late answers, so its timeout counts are weak evidence
findings.evidence:
Run 1 (23:23-23:25, about 12 java processes from concurrent auditors):
- vs boss: 40 games, 0 timeouts, maxFirst 649.1 ms, maxLater 47.3 ms.
- vs v00: 40 games, 2 first-turn timeouts (seed 6 seat 1; seed 11 seat 0), maxFirst 1021.2 ms.
- vs v01 (seedBase 101): 1 later-turn timeout (seed 103 seat 1), maxLater 61.8 ms, with no SLOW line from the bot.

None came back: run 2 used the same v00 seeds and had maxFirst 181.9 ms, and AuditRun run A covered seeds 101-120 with max later turn 14.17 ms.

The first turn includes JVM start, because the process starts just before the first input (Referee.java:120-124, 138). Artifact first turn over 150 games: p50 140.5 ms, p90 225.1, max 613.4. Interleaved baselines: minimal Java bot p50 109.7, max 290.0 (150 games); CG-template Scanner bot p50 171.9, max 447.2 (run A). So first-turn timeouts under load would hit any Java bot, not just this one.

Run 2 vs v00 also reported maxLater=148.2 ms with timeouts=0. Two mechanisms explain this:
- After the deadline, ProcessBot.readLine falls back to lines.poll() (ProcessBot.java:69-72), and LinkedBlockingQueue.poll(timeout) still dequeues a line that arrived while the thread was waking. A late answer can therefore pass.

I found no reachable path to an illegal command or a referee warning for the shipped bot. Static reading of MainBot against Command.parse, the Kotlin referee parser and Rules shows every line it can print is legal. Every warning in Rules is unreachable with the shipped Params (one knight barracks).

The bot played about 6,900 games in total: 5,900 in process and 980 as the real merged Player.java. In all of them it got 0 warnings, 0 protocol kills, 0 exceptions, 0 malformed lines and 0 extra stdout lines. verdicts.notes:
Verdict: real. The facts in the finding hold, and the line references (1164, 1190-1200, 1203, 1210-1211, 1217, 1226, 56) are correct.

Corrections and nuances to the finding:
1. Turn 1 pays the bootstrap in about 85% of games (1690 of 2000 maps touch a site on turn 0), not in every game. In the rest, the cost moves to turn 0, which has 1000 ms.
2. The first-threat turn pays the threat-lambda bootstrap in essentially every game. The first MOVE also pays a new string-concatenation shape; 75-80% of games ever MOVE.
3. "Not from the JIT" holds only on many cores. On one CPU, JIT compilation competes with the main thread and doubles the stall (-Xint 6.3 ms against JIT 14.0 ms, p50).
4. The quoted 45 ms comes from an overloaded run that also timed out on turn 0, so it is not typical. Still, under load the bootstrap turns are the ones that approach the limit: both SLOW lines in the legality corpus fall on them.

Why medium and not high:
- With JDK 17, no turn reached 50 ms in about 800 of my games across every configuration.
- CodinGame's hardware is unknown.
- The stall consumes 25-80% of the 50 ms budget on a single core, depending on core speed (p50 12-33 ms, max up to 39.5 ms). Each game exposes 2 turns, and a timeout means a lost game. That makes a loss plausible but not certain.
- If CodinGame moves to Java 25 (users request it), the first-MOVE stall roughly doubles (p50 28.9 ms on one E-core) and exceeded 50 ms in 2 of 45 games.

The suggested fix works. My independent warm-up (three play() calls on state copies on turn 0, before printing) removes the stall in every configuration:
- Turn 1 max: 0.6-1.0 ms on most configurations, 4.98 ms on the 1-CPU P-core.
- First MOVE max: 1.27 ms or less.
- Outputs identical in all 370 paired games.
- Turn 0 gets 13-44 ms slower at p50, well within 1000 ms.

I did not test the alternative fix (plain loops plus StringBuilder).

Minor aside: the "SLOW turn" message on stderr (Player.java:1270) is itself a new string-concatenation shape. It runs only after a slow turn's answer has been flushed, so it can add a few ms to the next turn. The warm-up does not cover it.
